name: Tumbao bass
rationale: The salsa and Latin pop tumbao: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the 'and' of 2 and on beat 4. That leaves the downbeat to the percussion and gives Latin songs their forward lean. In a real tumbao the beat-4 note anticipates the next chord. Here every note takes the chord sounding at its own beat, so beat 4 plays the current root and the fifth falls on the 'and' of 2. Four takes: classic (fifth then root), with a held root on 1 for entering a section, a root-octave version, and a sparser verse take.

name: Reggaeton bass
rationale: A reggaeton bass that locks to the dembow: short notes on beat 1, the 'a' of 1 (three 16ths later) and the 'and' of 2, repeated in each half-bar. The bass then pushes with the snare instead of fighting it. Three takes: all roots; a fifth below on the off-hits; and one that holds a long root through the second half of bar 2 to breathe.

name: Soul / Motown bass
rationale: The bouncing soul bass of Motown and of today's soul-pop. It uses root, octave and fifth with a dotted figure: a long root on 1, a pickup 16th before beat 2, the octave popping on the 'and' of 2, and the fifth walking back to the root. It moves more than a pumping pop bass without leaving the chord, because only root, fifth and octave are used and those fit every chord. Four takes, from busy to laid back.

name: Ballad held bass with pickups
rationale: How a bassist plays a slow ballad: long roots that let the chord ring, re-struck on beat 3 so they follow chords that change mid-bar, plus a short fifth or octave pickup into the next bar for a gentle push. It is quieter than a pop bass but still moves the song forward. Four takes: half notes; whole notes with a pickup; root then fifth-below; and dotted half plus an octave pickup.

name: Rock driving bass with fills
rationale: Straight-eighth rock bass, the engine of most guitar rock, with a short root-fifth-octave turn at the end of bar 2 to lead into the next phrase, as a bassist would. Four takes: plain eighths with an octave turnaround; eighths with an octave jump on the 'and' of 4; a galloping eighth-and-two-sixteenths take for the chorus; and half-time quarters for verses.

name: R&B / neo-soul bass
rationale: A laid-back R&B and neo-soul bass. It plays behind the beat: a root on 1, a late 16th push before beat 3, and the octave answering on the 'a' of 3. It leaves space for the vocal, unlike the urban generator's long 808 notes. Three takes: sparse; with a fifth-below approach; and a fuller version with a short octave-and-back turn.
